messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Redirection: I think of something else
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Dr. Eduardo Ramirez, a 62-year-old psychiatrist who has practiced in the United States for nearly two decades, still measures time by the year he was taken. Back then he was a young doctor in his home country, not yet gray at the temples, not yet scanning every room for exits. The men who came for him wore uniforms—military police, he learned later, though no charges were ever read. They held him for three weeks in a concrete room where the only sound was the incomprehensible chatter of guards speaking a dialect he could not parse, a stream of syllables that meant nothing and yet predicted everything—the blows, the hood, the moments when he was made to stand for hours until his legs gave. Some parts of that period remain etched in full, unbearable clarity: the taste of blood and diesel, the pressure of a boot on his throat, the exact pitch of a guard’s laugh. Other parts are blank—whole afternoons, faces, even the name of the man who finally unlocked the door and told him to leave. He never learned whether those responsible faced any consequences. The institution that should have protected its citizens had been the one holding the electrodes.

After his release, he left the country within a month. In the United States, Eduardo rebuilt his life slowly, earning his medical credentials again, passing board exams, securing a position at a community mental health clinic. He chose psychiatry because he believed in the mind’s capacity to heal. He still believes that, in principle. But he has also learned how stubbornly the mind can refuse.

Now, twenty-three years later, the memory returns without warning. It can happen while he is walking through the hospital cafeteria and hears a cluster of Spanish-speaking staff talking too fast for him to follow—not their words, but the rhythm, the unintelligible cheerfulness that turns suddenly alien. His throat tightens, his mouth fills with the phantom taste of blood, and for a few seconds he is back in the concrete room, all senses firing at once. He has learned to redirect: he thinks of something else, a patient’s medication list, a parking ticket he needs to pay, anything. But the cost of these redirections is mounting. He rehearses conversations now before every interaction, even with nurses he has known for years. What will he say? What will they ask? He runs through the possibilities in his mind, exhausting himself before the exchange has even begun. Going out has become a negotiation. He avoids the subway because of the crowds, the unidentifiable chatter, the occasional transit police officer whose uniform triggers a full-body freeze. He takes his car whenever possible, plotting routes that bypass government buildings and police stations.

At work, Eduardo is still competent, but his colleagues have noticed that he no longer attends department meetings if the agenda mentions new security protocols or police partnership initiatives. He cannot explain why without revealing too much, so he offers vague excuses about scheduling conflicts. The clinic administrator, a well-meaning woman who has never asked about his history, once left a newspaper on the break-room table with a front-page article about police reforms in Central America. Eduardo saw the headline from across the room and felt the floor tilt. He picked up the paper and threw it in the trash, then spent the next hour in his office with the door closed, using his redirection technique until the shaking stopped.

What Eduardo has come to believe, quietly, is that he no longer belongs anywhere. The community he grew up in—the music, the food, the easy trust among neighbors—was stolen from him. The country he fled is not his home, and the country that received him was never really offered as one. The institutions he once believed in—the medical board, the legal system, the very idea of justice—proved hollow. No one was held accountable for what happened to him. No one ever will be. He has not spoken Spanish with a patient in years, though he could; it feels too close to the voices that tormented him.

He came to therapy because a junior colleague referred him after he cancelled three consecutive clinic days following a news report about an immigration raid. Eduardo told himself he was just tired. But the colleague, who had read his file, said gently, “Maybe it’s time.” He sat in the intake chair with his hands folded, rehearsed his opening line one last time, and said, “I don’t know if this will help. But I can’t keep losing days.” What he does not say, but what he fears most, is that his mind will keep pulling him back to that room until there is nothing left of the life he built afterward.
